newsitem.title: UK: UK minister praises advertising self-regulation.
newsitem.headline: UK minister praises advertising self-regulation.

text.p: A British minister on Tuesday ruled out introducing statutory regulation of the advertising industry in the foreseeable future, saying the existing self-regulatory system adequately protected consumers.
Nigel Griffiths, the consumer affairs minister, told a gathering of business executives the government believed self regulation was more effective and cheaper than statutory regulation.
"I am a great believer in self regulation (of the advertising industry)," he told a luncheon organised by the Incorporated Society of British Advertisers (ISBA).
"It (statutory regulation) is expensive. It's slow. It's cumbersome. It's often over-reactive and it promotes litigation," he said.

There is heated debate across Europe about whether the advertising industry should be allowed to regulate itself, as happens in Britain, the Netherlands, Belgium and Switzerland, or whether the government should have more oversight, as takes place in Germany and France.

Advertising executives told Reuters that Griffith's comments were good news, particularly since some people in the industry had feared Britain's Labour Party would push for tighter advertising regulation after its leader, Tony Blair, was swept to power in a landslide victory on May 1.

Britain's Conservative Party, which held office for 18 years until its shattering defeat in May, had been considered friendlier towards the advertising industry than the Labour Party, and more willing to let the industry regulate itself.
Griffiths said on Tuesday it made more sense to leave oversight of the industry to Britain's Advertising Standards Authority, a self-regulatory body.
But he said in a written statement released on Tuesday that his ministry would take action if self-regulation was ever seen not working.
"I have no plans to bring in new controls on British advertising, but I am determined to act if self regulation fails to protect consumers," Griffiths said.

The government formed by Tony Blair, the head of the Labour Party, after he became prime minister in May, has already announced it plans to ban tobacco advertising and sponsorship of sporting events by tobacco companies.

British Home Secretary Jack Straw also launched an urgent ministerial inquiry in May into the consumption of so-called "alcopops", fruit-flavoured alcoholic drinks, which some consumer groups say have contributed to drunkenness and crime among young people.

"There must be no doubt that the government stands ready to act in specific cases -- whether it be health grounds vis-a-vis tobacco advertising or public interest grounds with alcopops, or in cases of particular abuse or sectors which prove themselves unable to accept the responsibilities which the freedom of self regulation brings," Griffiths said in the statement.
He told the ISBA luncheon the drinks industry had got itself into a "perceived mess" about alcopops, but that it was seriously trying to resolve the situation.

Consumer groups have accused companies that make alcopops of purposely targeting people under the legal drinking age of 18 by using marketing, including labelling and packaging, to attract young people.
"The (drinks) industry is now addressing these issues very seriously... We (the government) want to help the industry get out of the perceived mess it's got itself into," Griffiths said.
He urged drinks companies to adhere to an industry code created by the Portman Group, a self-regulatory body set up by drinks companies.
Griffiths also said the government would move gradually towards its planned ban of tobacco sponsorship of sporting events.
"It has got to be done in a way that does not damage sports. So there will be a transition period," he said.
"Our government is very sensitive to the concerns of British sports. We want to see Formula One continue on British television," Griffiths said.

Car racing experts say a ban on sponsorship by tobacco companies would hurt the finances of Formula One, the world's most glamorous and expensive motor racing event, and could force cutbacks in races or their transfer to Asia or other regions that do not restrict tobacco sponsorship.
